opus-5.5.text:
I don't actually see much tension between the two over the long run. When I think about the businesses I've helped build, whether it was Coursera, DeepLearning.AI, Landing AI, or the companies we incubate at AI Fund, the ones that endure are the ones that are obsessed with whether the customer is actually better off.

In the short term, sure, there are moments where you could squeeze a little more revenue out of someone, or push a product that isn't quite what they need. But I've found that if you consistently do the thing that genuinely helps the customer, the business tends to follow. Customers can tell when you're on their side. They come back, they tell their friends, they trust you with bigger problems. That compounding trust is worth far more than any short-term win.

With AI specifically, I feel this even more strongly. A lot of companies right now are trying to figure out how to use AI, and frankly there's a lot of hype. It would be easy to sell people on something flashy that doesn't really move the needle for them. But what I try to do, and what I encourage the teams I work with to do, is ask: what is the concrete value this creates? Does it save someone time, make them money, help them do something they couldn't do before? If you can't answer that clearly, you probably shouldn't be selling it.

So my mental model is that the business winning is a consequence of the customer winning. If I ever found myself in a situation where those two were really in conflict for a sustained period, I'd take that as a sign that something about the business model is broken and needs to be rethought.

r001.rationale: The response says business success tends to follow from helping customers. It does not state that entrepreneurs who prioritize their own business winning can nevertheless build successful businesses.

r002.rationale: The response mentions Coursera but says nothing about Andrew Ng’s behavior in its early days or whether he was motivated more by serving learners than by competition.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, I actually don't think of those as being in tension most of the time. If you go back to first principles, a business wins by creating value for someone and capturing a fraction of it. So if you're not making your customers win, you're not going to win for very long either.

Where I see teams get into trouble is when they optimize for short-term metrics that look like winning but aren't. You can juice engagement, you can lock people in, you can make something hard to cancel, and the dashboards go up for a quarter or two. But you've borrowed against your customers' trust, and eventually that comes due. I've seen that pattern enough times that I'm pretty skeptical of growth that isn't anchored in someone actually being better off.

At DeepLearning.AI, with Coursera before that, and with the companies we've started out of AI Fund, the question I keep coming back to is pretty simple: did we help this person do something they couldn't do before? Did a learner get a job? Did a company ship a product that works? When the answer is yes, the business side tends to take care of itself, and when the answer is no, no amount of clever monetization fixes it.

The one place where I do think there's real tension is around what the business can afford to do. There are things that would be great for customers that just don't have a sustainable model behind them. In those cases I think you have to be honest about it rather than pretend. But I'd much rather be in the position of saying "we'd love to do that and we're figuring out how to pay for it" than "we figured out how to pay for it and we're hoping customers don't notice what it costs them."

And honestly, in AI right now, there's so much genuine value to be created that I don't think anyone needs to resort to zero-sum thinking. The pie is growing fast. The teams I see doing best are the ones that stay close to users, find a real problem, solve it well, and let the business follow from that.

r001.rationale: The response says business and customer success are usually aligned: a business wins by creating value for customers, and the business follows when customers are better off.

r002.rationale: It mentions Coursera and serving learners, but does not describe Andrew Ng’s behavior in Coursera’s early days or compare that motivation with competition.

astra-6.text:
I think the best way to make your business win is to help your customers win. But you have to be specific about what that means. If we deliver a piece of software, that’s an output. Did it actually help someone do their job better, reduce costs, or serve their own customers better? That’s the outcome we should care about.

There can be tension in the short term. You might have an opportunity to sell something that a customer doesn’t really need. That helps this quarter’s revenue, but it’s a poor foundation for a business. I’d much rather be able to say, “I don’t think you need this yet. Here’s the problem I would work on first.”

The business still needs to capture enough value to keep investing and serving customers. So I don’t see these as two independent goals. The challenge is to build a business where customer success is what drives your success.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the two are closely connected, but they can diverge in the short term. You can make a sale that’s good for your revenue this quarter and doesn’t really help the customer. But I don’t think that’s a great foundation for a business.

The question I’d rather ask is: Can we make the customer successful, and then build a business that captures some of the value we create? That forces you to understand what they actually need. With AI, for example, delivering a model isn’t necessarily success. Success might mean their team saves time or they can serve their customers better. You have to follow through to that outcome.

Of course, you also need a sustainable business. If you can’t afford to keep improving the product and supporting customers, that doesn’t help them either. So I’d try to align those incentives: when our customers do better, we do better.

r001.rationale: The response says a business can capture value by making customers successful, but does not state that entrepreneurs prioritizing their own business winning can nevertheless build successful businesses.
